9/12/2026, 12:24:02 AM

That accounting is the right reset. I’m dropping every “almost-clue” that only restates the mathematics and focusing on the three unresolved primary targets: Temple of Music p. 161, the 1617 World Monochord F/F♯ geometry, and Fludd’s full 1622 answer to Analysis XXV mapped back onto the 1617 plate.

The key test is now stronger: a real clue should do more than mention a semitone or 81; it should connect location + correction + transition in a way that predicts where to look next.

Locating exact pages

I’m narrowing the visual analysis to identifiable first-edition pages, especially the world-monochord and temple-of-music engravings. I’m checking scans and page references so I can distinguish original layouts from later facsimiles.

Located exact pages

Refining page identification

I’m correcting the pagination issue: the “Temple of Music” material may belong to a different tract or volume than initially assumed. I’m separating scan-image numbering from printed pagination before drawing conclusions.

Refined page identification

Resolving pagination

I’m tracing adjacent scan pages because the engraving may sit between unnumbered plates and printed leaves. I’m comparing the title, folio sequence, and facing-page arrangement before identifying the image’s exact bibliographic location.

Resolved pagination

Searched 10 websites

Used python tool

Comparing source images

I’m comparing the supplied plate with high-resolution reproductions and adjacent leaves from the first edition. The key questions are whether “81” belongs to the engraving itself and how its surrounding labels establish the diagram’s meaning.

Compared source images

Searching the web

Tracing numerical symbolism

I’m now focusing on the “81” inscription itself: whether it denotes a Pythagorean ratio, a square-number progression, or a positional marker within the temple’s musical architecture.

Traced numerical symbolism

Examining numerical context

I’m checking the surrounding prose for how the engraving’s numbers function. The text emphasizes that every architectural element carries musical meaning, so “81” needs interpretation within the whole proportional system, not in isolation.

Examined numerical context

Connecting the architecture

I’m finding that the surrounding text treats the temple as an integrated mnemonic of natural, square, and proportional relationships. I’m checking later musical sections to see whether “81” belongs to that system or marks a separate numerical layer.

Connected the architecture

Testing the hypothesis

I’m checking whether “81” is part of the monochord’s ratio column rather than the solmization labels. That distinction matters: it could indicate a harmonic proportion, not a note or positional code.

Tested the hypothesis

Searched 7 websites

Separating ratio systems

I’m distinguishing Fludd’s architectural mnemonic from Kepler’s numerical harmonics. “81” may belong to a proportional monochord sequence, while “mi–fa” belongs to solmization; their visual proximity doesn’t prove they encode the same value.

Assessing the clue

I’m treating the temple engraving as a structured index rather than a decorative illustration. Its prose explicitly directs attention to spatial placement, so “81” should be read by location and neighboring labels before assigning symbolic meaning.

Separated ratio systems

Testing the notation link

I’m comparing the temple’s spatial labels with Fludd’s later solmization discussion, especially the mi–fa boundary. I’m checking whether the engraving encodes musical relationships directly rather than merely displaying proportional numbers.

Tested the notation link

Tracking foldout structure

I’m finding that the first-edition temple image involves folded or inserted leaves, which explains mismatches between printed pagination and scan order. I’m treating the engraving’s unfolded layout as primary evidence, not assuming each visible panel is a separate page.

Tracked foldout structure
